screens.title: Bring Up and Tear Down the test-network
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to bring a complete Hyperledger Fabric test network online, interact with it, and then tear it down safely. We will rely on the test-network's network. sh script as the single entry point that chains together cryptographic material generation, channel configuration, and Docker Compose orchestration. You will see how the up command runs cryptogen and configtxgen, how containers appear when you confirm with docker ps, and how createChannel and deployCC put a channel and chaincode in place so you can invoke transactions. You'll also practice the down command to remove containers and generated artifacts so your environment remains clean. Understanding these commands matters because fabric development iterates rapidly — a reproducible start and clean teardown protect you from stale identities, conflicting ports, and leftover ledger data. As you work, notice common pitfalls such as permission errors, Docker not running, and port conflicts so you can diagnose failures quickly. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to run the full cycle: up, verify, create channel, deploy chaincode, and down, with confidence and clear troubleshooting steps if something goes wrong.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on diagnostic skills and environment hygiene. You will learn to recognize typical failure signals such as Docker not running, permission denied when executing network. sh, and port conflicts that prevent container ports from binding. Each diagnosis has straightforward checks: confirm your Docker daemon is active before you run the script, verify network. sh has execute permissions with chmod if needed, and inspect docker-compose mappings to find port collisions. You'll also practice listing containers to confirm the exact names Fabric creates so you can match expected services when troubleshooting. Finally, you will understand why teardown matters: removing generated identities and ledger data fixes intermittent failures and ensures reproducibility for CI or subsequent demos. These troubleshooting habits reduce wasted time and give you confidence when the script output is verbose — you will know which lines to scan and which corrective steps to take.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Diagnostics & Troubleshooting
Common failure checks
Docker not running
Ensure Docker Desktop or daemon is active before running network.sh.
Permission denied
Make network.sh executable with chmod +x network.sh and confirm Docker access rights.
Port conflicts
Check compose port mappings and running services that might use Fabric ports such as 7050, 7051.
Quick diagnostic commands
Use these commands to gather the most useful evidence quickly before changing configuration.
# Check Docker status
docker ps -a

# Make network.sh executable
chmod +x network.sh

# Inspect port usage on Linux/macOS
lsof -i :7051

# Inspect Docker Compose mappings
# Open docker/docker-compose-test-net.yaml and look for port entries

screens.title: What network.sh orchestrates
screens.narratorSegment: network. sh is a convenience wrapper that sequences multiple Fabric tools so you can create a working local topology with a single command. At its core the script executes three tightly related stages: cryptographic material generation, genesis block and channel configuration generation, and container orchestration via Docker Compose. Cryptogen reads the crypto-config. yaml and emits certificates and keys for Organizations, peers, orderers, and CAs. Configtxgen then uses configtx. yaml to create the orderer's genesis block and channel configuration transactions. Finally Docker Compose brings up orderer, peers, certificate authorities, and optional CouchDB instances as containers based on the YAML files under the docker directory. A concrete example: when you run./network. sh up, you will see cryptogen produce an organizations folder, configtxgen create a system-genesis-block directory, and Docker create containers named peer0. org1. example. com, peer0. org2. example. com, and orderer. example. com. A common misconception is thinking network. sh is an installer; it does not download binaries or replace prerequisites. It expects the Fabric tools and a running Docker environment. Keep that in mind and confirm prerequisites before running the script. The core takeaway is that network. sh combines deterministic artifact generation with container startup so you get a repeatable local network each run.

keyIdea.title: Three-stage orchestration
keyIdea.text: network.sh sequences cryptogen, configtxgen, and Docker Compose to produce a running, reproducible local Fabric topology.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › What network.sh orchestrates
Process overview
1. Generate crypto (cryptogen)
Produces certificates and keys defined in crypto-config.yaml for organizations, peers, orderers and CAs.
2. Create genesis & channel tx (configtxgen)
Creates the system genesis block and channel configuration transactions from configtx.yaml.
3. Start containers (Docker Compose)
Brings up orderer, peers, and CAs in containers so the network is reachable for channel and chaincode actions.
Key Takeaway

network.sh bundles deterministic artifact generation with container orchestration to produce a reproducible local network quickly.

Terminal-first example
cd ~/fabric-dev/fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh up

# Expect outputs from cryptogen, configtxgen, and then Docker creating containers
Concrete expectation: after the script completes, look for an organizations folder, a system-genesis-block folder, and Docker containers named peer0.org1.example.com, peer0.org2.example.com, and orderer.example.com.
Common misconception
network.sh is not an installer. It assumes Fabric tools and Docker are already installed and available in your PATH.

screens.title: Generate Cryptographic Material
screens.narratorSegment: Generating cryptographic material is the first essential step when starting the test-network. cryptogen reads the crypto-config. yaml file to produce the organizations directory containing certificates and private keys for each organization, its peers, and the orderer. These artifacts implement the fabric public key infrastructure that identities and MSPs rely on. For example, when cryptogen runs during./network. sh up you will see directories like organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/peers/peer0. org1. example. com/msp with certificates and keys. A common mistake is to assume certificates are persistent across runs; network. sh up regenerates material unless artifacts are already present or you have a workflow that preserves them. Another pitfall is file permissions — private keys must remain readable by the processes that need them; if you see permission denied errors, check ownership and execution context. The practical significance is this: identities determine who can sign, endorse, and perform administrative actions. If certificates are missing or invalid, the orderer and peers cannot form a proper channel or validate transactions. Always confirm organizations/ exists after cryptogen and inspect the expected msp folders before moving to configtxgen and Docker startup.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Generate Cryptographic Material
What cryptogen does
  • Reads crypto-config.yaml to learn organization and peer definitions.
  • Emits certificates and private keys into organizations/ with MSP folder structure.
  • Creates identities used by peers, orderer, and administration tools.
Example output
/fabric-samples/test-network/organizations/
├─ peerOrganizations/
│  └─ org1.example.com/
│     └─ peers/peer0.org1.example.com/msp
└─ ordererOrganizations/
Checks & common mistakes
• Ensure organizations/ exists after running cryptogen. If missing, cryptogen failed earlier.
• Permission issues: verify the user running Docker and scripts can read private keys.
• Do not assume artifacts persist across runs; network.sh down may delete them, and up may regenerate them.
Key Takeaway

Cryptographic artifacts are foundational for identity and must exist and be accessible before channel creation and chaincode deployment.

screens.title: Genesis Block and Channel Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: configtxgen creates two kinds of artifacts: the system genesis block that initializes the ordering service and channel configuration transactions that define a channel's initial policies and member organizations. The genesis block anchors the ordering service: without it the orderer cannot start correctly. Channel configuration transactions are later used to create channels with a defined set of members and policies. For example, when you run network. sh up you will see a system-genesis-block directory containing the genesis. block. Later, when you invoke./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel the script uses the channel transaction to create mychannel and register the peers and orderer in its configuration. A common misunderstanding is treating genesis and channel artifacts interchangeably. They are distinct: genesis is for the orderer system, while channel transactions target a named communication subnet between organizations. Practically, if configtxgen fails, the orderer or channel creation will fail and containers may not reach a ready state. Confirm that system-genesis-block exists and that createChannel runs without error before deploying chaincode. This ensures the network has the necessary ordering and membership structures to validate transactions. Genesis Block and Channel Configuration means configtxgen produces the orderer's genesis block and channel transactions — both required for a functioning ordering service and channels.. In practical terms, what configtxgen produces and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Orderer genesis vs channel tx
keyIdea.text: configtxgen produces the orderer's genesis block and channel transactions — both required for a functioning ordering service and channels.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Genesis & Channel Config
Artifacts created by configtxgen
• system-genesis-block/genesis.block initializes the ordering service.
• Channel configuration transactions define initial channel members and policies.
Example file
/fabric-samples/test-network/system-genesis-block/genesis.block
/fabric-samples/test-network/channel-artifacts/mychannel.tx
Why the distinction matters
  • Genesis block boots the ordering service; without it, orderer container cannot form a ledger.
  • Channel transactions are applied to create a private ledger between specified orgs.
  • Treat failures in either stage as blockers for channel creation and chaincode deployment.
Misconception check

Do not assume a successful cryptogen implies configtxgen succeeded. Both must complete for a valid network.

screens.title: Starting the Docker containers
screens.narratorSegment: After cryptographic and genesis artifacts exist, the script invokes Docker Compose to start the ordering service, peers, CAs, and optional CouchDB instances. These services are declared in YAML files inside the test-network's docker directory. When Docker Compose runs, it creates container names you can inspect with docker ps -a. For example, peer0. org1. example. com represents the first peer for Org1 and orderer. example. com represents the single Raft orderer used in the test-network. A concrete command sequence you will execute is: change into the test-network folder and run./network. sh up. If containers fail to start, Docker Compose output will show which containers exited and often include port-binding or dependency errors. A frequent oversight is not running Docker as a daemon or using an account without Docker permissions; this produces immediate failures. Another nuance is optional CouchDB: if enabled, you will also see couchdb0 and couchdb1 containers. The practical check is to run docker ps -a and confirm container names and statuses are as expected before proceeding to channel creation. If a container is restarting or exited, inspect its logs to find the cause and resolve configuration or port conflicts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Starting Containers
Code walkthrough — start sequence
cd ~/fabric-dev/fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh up

# Watch for cryptogen and configtxgen output, then Docker Compose creating containers
Look for containers named: peer0.org1.example.com, peer0.org2.example.com, orderer.example.com, ca_org1, ca_org2, ca_orderer. Optional CouchDB containers: couchdb0, couchdb1.
Inspecting containers
docker ps -a
# Expect entries with the Fabric container names listed above
If containers are exited, view logs to diagnose: docker logs <container-name>. Typical errors include port already in use or configuration problems preventing the orderer from starting.
Pro-tip
Keep a terminal open to stream logs during startup so you can catch the first failing service and fix it quickly.

screens.title: Verify the network with docker ps
screens.narratorSegment: Verifying that the test-network is running is a simple but crucial step. The docker ps -a command lists running and stopped containers and is your primary evidence that peers, orderer, and certificate authorities have started successfully. After running./network. sh up, run docker ps -a --format "table {{. ID}}\t{{. Names}}\t{{. Status}}" to get a readable table of containers. You should see peer0. org1. example. com, peer0. org2. example. com, orderer. example. com, ca_org1, ca_org2, and ca_orderer. If you configured CouchDB you will also see couchdb0 and couchdb1. A concrete example: if peer0. org1. example. com shows Up for a few minutes, that peer is likely healthy; if it shows Exited or Restarting, follow the logs to identify port binding or permission issues. A common misconception is assuming running containers always mean the network is ready; some containers may be up but failing initialization internally. Check logs for errors and ensure cryptographic artifacts and the genesis block exist before creating a channel. The key step is to treat docker ps as an early validation and follow up with targeted log checks when anything is not in the expected Running state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Verify with docker ps
Run this verification
docker ps -a --format "table {{.ID}}  {{.Names}}  {{.Status}}"

# Confirm names: peer0.org1.example.com, peer0.org2.example.com, orderer.example.com, ca_org1, ca_org2, ca_orderer
Healthy
Status: Up — proceed to create a channel.
Exited
Check docker logs <name> to see why it stopped during initialization.
Restarting
Likely a crash loop; inspect logs and port binding conflicts.
Key Takeaway

docker ps is your first line of defense to confirm the network is present; follow up with logs when statuses are not Running.

screens.title: Create a Channel
screens.narratorSegment: Channels let a subset of network participants maintain a private ledger. The test-network script simplifies channel creation using the createChannel command. The typical usage is./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel where -c specifies the channel name. Under the hood the command submits the channel creation transaction produced by configtxgen to the ordering service; peers then join the channel and the necessary ledger is created on those peers. A concrete example is creating mychannel between Org1 and Org2 so that chaincode state and transactions are visible only to those members. Common misconceptions include thinking channels are automatic after startup; they require this explicit creation step. Another pitfall is trying to create a channel before the genesis block and ordering service are ready — ensure orderer and peers are running and that system-genesis-block exists. If createChannel fails, inspect the script output for endorsement policy mismatches or connection failures to the orderer. Once the channel is created and peers have joined, you can deploy chaincode and invoke application transactions confined to that channel. Create a Channel means createchannel submits the channel configuration to the orderer and causes peers to join a shared private ledger for specific organizations.. In practical terms, use network.sh createchannel to form a private communication subnet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Create a Channel
Command
./network.sh createChannel -c mychannel
This submits the channel transaction to the ordering service and instructs peers to join the new channel, creating a private ledger for the named members.
Checks & examples
  • Confirm orderer is running and system-genesis-block exists before creating a channel.
  • If creation fails, inspect orderer logs and check peer connectivity information.
  • After successful creation, use peer lifecycle commands or the script to install and commit chaincode to the channel.
Why it matters
Channels provide confidentiality and separate ledgers for different consortium subsets—without them every transaction would be visible to all network members.

screens.title: Deploy Chaincode with deployCC
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying chaincode is a multi-step lifecycle that network. sh helps automate with deployCC. The script handles packaging the chaincode source, installing it on peers, collecting approvals from organizations, and committing the definition so chaincode becomes active on the channel. A common invocation from the test-network is:./network. sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go -ccl go. Here -ccn names the chaincode, -ccp indicates the path to source, and -ccl specifies the runtime language. Concretely, deployCC packages the Go chaincode into a tarball, installs it onto each peer container, runs the approval steps that register the chaincode definition across orgs, and finally commits so invocations are accepted. screens.title: Common startup failures and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: When network. sh fails, three failure modes dominate: Docker not running, permission or execution errors for the script, and port conflicts that prevent containers from binding. Docker not running is straightforward: the Docker daemon must be active. If you see low-level connection errors the script cannot reach the container runtime. Permission denied errors typically point to network. sh lacking execute permissions or the invoking user not having Docker privileges; remedy this with chmod +x network. sh and confirm Docker CLI access. Port conflicts cause Docker Compose to fail when a required host port is already in use. To diagnose ports, inspect the docker-compose-test-net YAML to see mapped ports and then query OS tools like lsof or netstat to find the occupying process. A concrete troubleshooting flow is: check Docker status, run docker ps -a to gather container state, inspect failing container logs with docker logs name, and confirm file permissions and port availability. A common misconception is editing Fabric compose ports casually; while possible, changing ports can lead to hidden mismatches in scripts and client tooling. Prefer stopping conflicting services or adjusting your local environment unless you understand all compose mappings. The final takeaway is a structured diagnostic approach: check Docker, verify permissions, and inspect port usage, in that order.

keyIdea.text: Check Docker, verify script permissions, and inspect ports in sequence to quickly identify startup failures.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Startup Failures
Docker not running
Check Docker Desktop or the Docker daemon. If not running, start it and re-run network.sh.
Permission denied
Run chmod +x network.sh and ensure your user can call Docker commands without sudo or adjust privileges.
Port conflicts
Inspect docker-compose mappings for ports like 7050 and 7051, then use OS tools to find the process occupying them.
Suggested diagnostic flow
  1. Confirm Docker daemon is active and accessible.
  2. Run docker ps -a to see container states and names.
  3. For Exited containers, run docker logs <name> to inspect error messages.
  4. Check file permissions for network.sh and generated keys.
  5. Inspect host port usage if compose cannot bind required ports.

screens.title: Tear down the network with ./network.sh down
screens.narratorSegment: When you finish experimenting, you must clean up the test-network to free resources and remove generated artifacts. The network. sh down command stops and removes all Docker containers started by the script, deletes generated cryptographic material under organizations/, removes the system genesis block, and cleans up chaincode images and ledger data. This step is important because leftover identities, ledger data, or port bindings can create confusing behavior in subsequent runs. For example, you might expect a fresh identity but find the old certificates still present; network. sh down prevents that. To run the cleanup, execute./network. sh down from the test-network directory. Verify cleanup by running docker ps -a and observing that the Fabric containers are no longer present and by inspecting that organizations/ and system-genesis-block/ are removed. A common misconception is that simply stopping containers is sufficient; network. sh down is preferred because it explicitly removes files created during up and ensures a repeatable start for future sessions. Use down before switching branches, changing network configurations, or recording demo output to avoid cross-run contamination. Tear down the network with ./network.sh down means network.sh down removes containers and all generated artifacts so you can reliably start a fresh test-network later.. In this chapter you'll learn how to bring a complete Hyperledger Fabric test network online, interact with it, and then tear it down safely. We will rely on the test-network's network. sh script as the single entry point that chains together cryptographic material generation, channel configuration, and Docker Compose orchestration. You will see how the up command runs cryptogen and configtxgen, how containers appear when you confirm with docker ps, and how createChannel and deployCC put a channel and chaincode in place so you can invoke transactions. You'll also practice the down command to remove containers and generated artifacts so your environment remains clean. Understanding these commands matters because fabric development iterates rapidly — a reproducible start and clean teardown protect you from stale identities, conflicting ports, and leftover ledger data. As you work, notice common pitfalls such as permission errors, Docker not running, and port conflicts so you can diagnose failures quickly. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to run the full cycle: up, verify, create channel, deploy chaincode, and down, with confidence and clear troubleshooting steps if something goes wrong.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to initialize a local Fabric test network using the provided network. sh script, verify the running components using Docker commands, create a channel, and deploy a sample chaincode. You will also be able to perform a clean teardown to remove containers and generated artifacts. Each objective focuses on practical skills: running network. sh up sequences the cryptographic generation and ordering service setup so you can reach a working peer topology. Verifying containers teaches you to read docker ps output and confirm peer, orderer, and CA services are active. Creating a channel and deploying chaincode teaches packaging, endorsement, and commit steps so your application logic can execute on the ledger. Finally, the teardown objective ensures you can reset your environment and avoid conflicts in later sessions. These competencies keep your development loop reproducible and avoid leftover identities or port collisions. You’ll practice commands, inspect outputs, and learn troubleshooting tactics for common failures.

This second objectives slide focuses on diagnostic skills and environment hygiene. You will learn to recognize typical failure signals such as Docker not running, permission denied when executing network. sh, and port conflicts that prevent container ports from binding. Each diagnosis has straightforward checks: confirm your Docker daemon is active before you run the script, verify network. sh has execute permissions with chmod if needed, and inspect docker-compose mappings to find port collisions. You'll also practice listing containers to confirm the exact names Fabric creates so you can match expected services when troubleshooting. Finally, you will understand why teardown matters: removing generated identities and ledger data fixes intermittent failures and ensures reproducibility for CI or subsequent demos. These troubleshooting habits reduce wasted time and give you confidence when the script output is verbose — you will know which lines to scan and which corrective steps to take.

network. sh is a convenience wrapper that sequences multiple Fabric tools so you can create a working local topology with a single command. At its core the script executes three tightly related stages: cryptographic material generation, genesis block and channel configuration generation, and container orchestration via Docker Compose. Cryptogen reads the crypto-config. yaml and emits certificates and keys for Organizations, peers, orderers, and CAs. Configtxgen then uses configtx. yaml to create the orderer's genesis block and channel configuration transactions. Finally Docker Compose brings up orderer, peers, certificate authorities, and optional CouchDB instances as containers based on the YAML files under the docker directory. A concrete example: when you run./network. sh up, you will see cryptogen produce an organizations folder, configtxgen create a system-genesis-block directory, and Docker create containers named peer0. org1. example. com, peer0. org2. example. com, and orderer. example. com. A common misconception is thinking network. sh is an installer; it does not download binaries or replace prerequisites. It expects the Fabric tools and a running Docker environment. Keep that in mind and confirm prerequisites before running the script. The core takeaway is that network. sh combines deterministic artifact generation with container startup so you get a repeatable local network each run.

Generating cryptographic material is the first essential step when starting the test-network. cryptogen reads the crypto-config. yaml file to produce the organizations directory containing certificates and private keys for each organization, its peers, and the orderer. These artifacts implement the fabric public key infrastructure that identities and MSPs rely on. A common mistake is to assume certificates are persistent across runs; network. sh up regenerates material unless artifacts are already present or you have a workflow that preserves them. Another pitfall is file permissions — private keys must remain readable by the processes that need them; if you see permission denied errors, check ownership and execution context. The practical significance is this: identities determine who can sign, endorse, and perform administrative actions. If certificates are missing or invalid, the orderer and peers cannot form a proper channel or validate transactions. Always confirm organizations/ exists after cryptogen and inspect the expected msp folders before moving to configtxgen and Docker startup.

configtxgen creates two kinds of artifacts: the system genesis block that initializes the ordering service and channel configuration transactions that define a channel's initial policies and member organizations. The genesis block anchors the ordering service: without it the orderer cannot start correctly. Channel configuration transactions are later used to create channels with a defined set of members and policies. For example, when you run network. sh up you will see a system-genesis-block directory containing the genesis. block. Later, when you invoke./network. sh createChannel -c mychannel the script uses the channel transaction to create mychannel and register the peers and orderer in its configuration. A common misunderstanding is treating genesis and channel artifacts interchangeably. They are distinct: genesis is for the orderer system, while channel transactions target a named communication subnet between organizations. Practically, if configtxgen fails, the orderer or channel creation will fail and containers may not reach a ready state. Confirm that system-genesis-block exists and that createChannel runs without error before deploying chaincode. This ensures the network has the necessary ordering and membership structures to validate transactions. For example, peer0. org1. example. com represents the first peer for Org1 and orderer. example. com represents the single Raft orderer used in the test-network.
